h1: The 7 Best Quiet NAS for Home Offices of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Quiet Home Office NAS 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: seven NAS options for quiet home offices, from the 2-bay Synology DS223 to a single-bay Buffalo, plus advice on bays and drives.
summary: The Synology DS223 is the best overall because two bays keep noise modest and its software schedules heavy work for overnight. The Beelink ME Pro is the quietest by design thanks to three M.2 SSD slots and a low-power CPU. TERRAMASTER leads on speed with 2.5GbE, and UGREEN's DXP2800 adds sustained-load cooling. The Buffalo is the simplest start.
intro: A NAS is quiet only while it idles. The sounds that drive people out of a home office come from two moments: drives spinning up and seeking, and fans ramping during a long transfer. Nobody can promise a silent box if hard drives are inside. None of the listings here publishes a decibel figure, so any reviewer quoting one is guessing, and we will not do the same.

In practice, we ranked seven storage boxes on the factors that actually decide noise in a small office: bay count, SSD capability, cooling design, how quickly transfers finish and whether heavy jobs can be moved overnight. Scores follow the Primea framework, using spec sheets and listing details only, with owner feedback treated as a hint about fan behaviour rather than a measurement.

products.name: Synology DS223 Home & Office Backup Hub (2-Bay Diskless NAS)
products.verdict: Mature software and overnight scheduling for a desk-side box.
products.description:
The Synology DS223 earns first place by being sensible about noise rather than claiming silence. It is a two-bay diskless NAS running Synology DSM, aimed at home and small offices, with file centralisation, backup and scheduled overnight tasks in the software. Two bays mean two drives, which limits the clatter compared with larger boxes.

It beats the Beelink on software maturity, and the TERRAMASTER on scheduling clarity, because the overnight task feature moves loud work such as indexing and backups away from your working hours. At $200 to $500 it lands in the same bracket as the other leaders.

Buy it for a home office that mostly backs up laptops and shares files. The honest caveat is that no decibel figure is published, and a diskless unit means the drive choice sets the noise. Pick quiet drives and leave it overnight.
products.idealFor: A desk-side backup box run mostly overnight.

products.name: Beelink Mini PC ME Pro, 2 Hard Drive Bays NAS
products.verdict: A low-power mini PC with three SSD slots for silent storage.
products.description:
The Beelink ME Pro is the closest thing to quiet in this ranking. It pairs an Intel N95 with 12GB LPDDR5, a 128GB M.2 PCIe 3.0 SSD, two hard drive bays and three M.2 slots, with dual LAN. The three M.2 slots are the story: SSDs have no moving parts, so a flash-only setup can run almost silent.

It ranks second because it is a mini PC working as a NAS rather than a dedicated appliance, so software and long-term support are less polished than the Synology. It sits in the $200 to $500 bracket and beats the TERRAMASTER on low-power design. Fill it with SSDs and it wins on noise outright.

Choose it for a desk where fan and drive sounds must be minimal. The caveat is capacity: SSD space costs far more per terabyte than spinning drives.
products.idealFor: People who put silence ahead of capacity.
products.skipIf: You want a polished NAS operating system.

products.name: TERRAMASTER F2-425 2-Bay NAS Storage
products.verdict: Quicker transfers mean the drives spend less time working.
products.description:
The TERRAMASTER F2-425 competes on speed. Two bays arrive empty, backed by an Intel x86 quad-core processor, 4GB RAM and a 2.5GbE port, and the box can serve multimedia. A faster port means transfers end sooner, so the drives and fan spend less time working during your day.

It ranks third because speed is only an indirect noise benefit. The 2.5GbE link needs a matching switch or computer port to deliver anything, and the listing publishes no cooling or sound detail. The Synology DS223 is easier to plan around thanks to its scheduling. The Asustor below also offers 2.5GbE for less money.

Buy it for large file moves such as footage or image libraries. The caveat is that you must supply 2.5GbE networking and drives, and noise is not described anywhere in the listing.
products.idealFor: Large file transfers that finish quickly.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP2800, 2-Bay for Content Creators
products.verdict: Cooling designed for sustained load, which can mean steadier fans.
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP2800 is a two-bay diskless NAS aimed at content creators, with cooling designed for sustained load stability and the UGREEN NAS OS ecosystem. Sustained load is when fan noise rises, so a design that holds temperatures steady can avoid the ramp up and down that is most irritating in a quiet room.

It ranks fourth because stability is not the same as quiet, and the listing states no fan noise figure. The Beelink gives you a quieter path through SSDs, while the Synology schedules loud tasks away from the workday. Against the DH2300 below, it costs more and targets heavier use.

Choose it if you edit video or handle large projects at the desk. The caveat is that creator-focused performance can mean more spinning and more heat, so give it ventilation and put it out of earshot.

products.name: Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 AS1202T, 2-Bay NAS
products.verdict: A lower-cost box that suits light, quiet backup duty.
products.description:
The Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 is the cheapest way here to get 2.5GbE. Inside are two bays, no drives, a 1.7GHz quad-core chip, 1GB DDR4 RAM and 4K media serving, all in the $100 to $200 bracket. A modest processor generates less heat, which helps the fan stay slow.

It ranks fifth because 1GB RAM is thin for multitasking, and the listing says nothing about scheduling or cooling. The TERRAMASTER above offers 4GB RAM and a more capable CPU in the $200 to $500 bracket. This one wins only on price.

Buy it for backup duty and light media serving on a tight budget. The caveat is memory: a 1GB machine will struggle if you pile on apps, and a busy NAS makes more noise as it works harder.
products.skipIf: You stream and transcode a lot.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DH2300, 2-Bay Desktop NAS (Diskless)
products.verdict: Plain two-bay storage with no creator extras.
products.description:
The UGREEN DH2300 is the simple two-bay option. It is a diskless desktop NAS supporting up to 64TB, with UGREEN NAS OS and a focus on backup and file sharing, in the $100 to $200 bracket. A backup-first design suits a quiet office because jobs can run on a timer.

It ranks sixth because it lists no 2.5GbE or processor detail, so you cannot judge its speed. Compared with the DXP2800 it costs less and aims lower, which is fine for light office duty. The Asustor adds 2.5GbE at a similar price.

Choose it for simple backups and file sharing in a small office. The caveat is that the listing does not describe cooling or fan behaviour, so check owner feedback on noise before relying on it near your desk.
products.skipIf: You want extra services or speed.

products.name: BUFFALO LinkStation 210 2TB, 1-Bay NAS (Drives Included)
products.verdict: A one-bay box with a 2TB drive already inside.
products.description:
The Buffalo LinkStation 210 is the single-bay beginner. It ships with a 2TB drive included, offers home cloud and file sharing, and sets up without a separate drive purchase, in the $100 to $200 bracket. One bay and one drive is the lowest mechanical noise you can get from a spinning NAS.

It ranks last because one bay means no redundancy: if the drive fails, your data is at risk unless you back up elsewhere. It also lists no 2.5GbE, scheduling or SSD support. Against the Synology DS223, you give up bays, software depth and growth.

Buy it for a home user who wants simple network storage and no shopping for drives. The caveat is that the included drive is the only choice you get, so you cannot swap to an SSD later.
products.idealFor: A first NAS with minimal setup.

whatMatters.detail: Hard drives spin and click, while SSDs have no moving parts and make no mechanical noise. A NAS with M.2 or SSD slots can run close to silent. The Beelink ME Pro lists three M.2 slots and two hard drive bays. Check the spec table for M.2 or SSD support before assuming the box can run quietly, and note whether the SSDs are included.

Each bay adds a drive and its noise. One or two bays keep sound down, while four or more bays add spinning drives and heavier cooling. Every NAS here has one or two bays. Check the bay count in the title, and remember a diskless unit lets you choose quieter drives, while an included drive limits you.

Constant video transcoding or heavy indexing makes fans ramp, while backup and file sharing are lighter. A NAS serving 4K media works harder than one copying files overnight. Match the hardware to your real jobs. If you only back up laptops, the Synology DS223 or UGREEN DH2300 is enough and generates less noise.

Moving heavy tasks overnight keeps noise away from working hours. Backups, indexing and maintenance can run on a timer when the office is empty. The Synology DS223 lists scheduled overnight tasks in its software. Look for scheduling features in the software description, and confirm that they cover backups and maintenance.

None of these listings publishes decibels, so treat quiet claims as design hints rather than facts. Look at owner feedback on fan ramp and drive clatter, and check whether the box uses SSDs or a low-power CPU. Never trust an unsourced dB number, because noise varies with drives, room and placement, and a box on a hard desk sounds louder than one on a shelf.

faq.q: Are any of these truly silent?
faq.a: Only an SSD-based setup comes close, such as the Beelink ME Pro with M.2 drives and no spinning platters. Hard drive models like the Synology DS223 always make some sound when working, especially during backups.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake with a quiet NAS?
faq.a: Trusting a quiet claim with no data behind it. None of these listings publish decibels, so judge the Beelink, Synology and UGREEN boxes by bay count, drive type and scheduling, then read owner comments on fan behaviour.

Indirectly, since faster transfers end sooner and the drives spend less time working. It needs matching network gear on both ends to deliver any speed gain. The TERRAMASTER F2-425 and Asustor AS1202T both list 2.5GbE, but a plain gigabit switch will cap them.

Only the BUFFALO LinkStation 210 lists a 2TB drive included. The Synology DS223, TERRAMASTER, UGREEN and Asustor models are diskless, so drive choice is yours and largely decides how much noise you hear at the desk.

faq.q: How do I schedule overnight tasks?
faq.a: The Synology DS223 supports scheduled overnight tasks in its software. Open DSM, find the backup and maintenance schedules, and set heavy jobs to run late at night so they finish well before you start work.

faq.q: Why not a USB storage box?
faq.a: A direct-attached unit like the QNAP TR-004 is not network-attached, so we left it out of the ranking. A true NAS such as the Synology DS223 shares files with every device on your network, which is the point.

finalTake: Choose the Synology DS223 if you want a proven, schedulable two-bay box. Pick the Beelink ME Pro when silence is the priority and you can live on SSDs. Take the TERRAMASTER F2-425 for faster transfers that end sooner. Remember that no listing publishes dB figures, so read owner feedback on fan behaviour and put the box where its noise can be shut away.
